claims.text: The restored source explicitly asks for two Goroutines to alternately print integers 1 through 100 in a Go/PHP backend interview context.
Go statements start independently executing goroutines; channels support communication among goroutines, and a capacity-one channel can hold the initial turn token.

The Go memory model defines channel operations as synchronization operations and states that a channel send is synchronized before completion of its corresponding receive, supporting the candidate's token-handoff ordering argument.

WaitGroup.Wait blocks until the counter is zero; Done decrements the counter; positive Add calls from zero should precede Wait and are typically performed before starting the goroutine. WaitGroup.Go was added in Go 1.25, so Add/Done remains compatible with earlier Go versions.
The exact implementation/test bytes pass go test -race under Go 1.23.2 in an isolated module; 100 repeated runs each emit exactly the ordered sequence 1 through 100 with no reported race or deadlock.

findings: The candidate uses Go Goroutines and channels, matching the restored source language boundary instead of reusing the old Java placeholder.
Turn ownership is explicit and deterministic; sleep and scheduler timing are not used as synchronization.
The final even iteration deliberately performs no further handoff, preventing the common terminal-send deadlock.
WaitGroup is used only for completion while channels establish ordering, keeping synchronization responsibilities separate.
The fixed implementation is covered by repeated exact-order assertions and the Go race detector.
Human approval is still required before promotion; this evidence does not fabricate that approval.
